Phase 5: Return to Performance

In Phase 5 of the CSI Pacific ACL Rehabilitation Protocol, the off-field components become secondary to on-field training, however the importance of these components does not diminish at all. The goal of this section is to help everyone involved with the rehab to navigate the complexities of returning to sport and to performance, while continuing to care for the knee with a high degree of attention to detail. Phase 5 will be highly individualized based on the sport that the athlete competes in, and while it is not possible to cover specific details for all sports, there remain principles and fundamentals which inform best practice during this critical phase. We hope that the resources provided in this chapter will make it easier to navigate these complexities by providing a highly organized and detailed road-map for continuing a successful rehab which supports improvements in on-field performance.

ImportantMost Important Goals — Phase 3
  • Performance on all dynamic tasks exceeds 95% of pre-injury or opposite leg performance

What does the research say?

“Completion of the rehabilitation protocol and clearance to return to sport is not the same as return to competition. Before clearance for return to unrestricted competition, there should be a transition phase from sports participation to sports performance with progressive and controlled exposure to athlete’s sport” [1]

It is important that training continues, and criteria are consistently re-evaluated as the athlete returns to regular training and competition.

Neuromuscular training returns to it’s place as being secondary to sport training. The athlete’s schedule is no longer built around what is optimal physiologically, rather it must be adapted to fit with the daily and weekly training schedules of the sport. For example, workouts may now occur following practices and games, when fatigue may play a factor in force production [2] or movement quality [3].

Continued testing of Phase 5 criteria are important for ensuring that the athlete does not compromise the physical, mental and emotional gains made throughout the rehab.

Warm Up

Is there research or dies this go in additional resources?

The warm-up becomes extremely crucial for this athlete for the rest of their career in order to optimally prepare for training/competition, and also as a n opportunity to target specific neuromuscular needs on a constant basis, and while feeling fresh before undergoing the demands of the sport.

Testing

Each card below contains a detailed description of the tests to be conducted during this phase of rehab.

Single Leg Hop

Athlete stands on one leg and hops as far forward as possible, landing on the same leg.

  • Measure from toe at take-off to heel at landing. Arms are free to swing. The athlete must demonstrate control by sticking the landing for a minimum of 3s.

The score for each limb is calculated as a mean of 2 successful reps. A limb symmetry index is calculated by dividing the mean distance (in cms) of the involved limb by the mean distance of the noninvolved limb then multiplying by 100

Criteria: ≥ 95%

Repetitions: 2

Calculation: Mean

Triple Hop

Athletes stands on one leg and hops forwards three consecutive times on one foot, sticking the final landing.

  • Measure from toe at take off to heel at landing. Arms are free to swing. The athlete must demonstrate control by sticking the final landing for a minimum of 3s.

The total distance is measured, and the mean of 2 valid tests is recorded. A limb symmetry index is calculated by dividing the mean distance (in cms) of the involved limb by the mean distance of the noninvolved limb then multiplying by 100.

Criteria: ≥ 95%

Repetitions: 2

Calculation: Mean

Triple Cross Over Hop

This test is performed on a course consisting of a 15cm marking strip on the floor which is 6m long. The athlete is required to hop three consecutive times on one foot going in a medial to lateral to medial direction, crossing the strip on each hop.

  • Measure from toe at take-off to heel at landing. Arms are free to swing. The athlete must demonstrate control by sticking the final landing for a minimum of 3s.

The total distance is measured, and the average (mean) of 2 valid hop tests is recorded. A limb symmetry index is calculated by dividing the mean distance (in cms) of the involved limb by the mean distance of the noninvolved limb then multiplying by 100.

Criteria: ≥ 95%

Repetitions: 2

Calculation: Mean

Side Hop

Subjects stands on test leg with hands behind the back and jumps from side to side between two parallel strips of tape, placed 40 cm apart on the floor. (Gustavsson et al., 2006)

  • Subject jumps as many times as possible during 30sec. The number of successful jumps performed, without touching the tape is recorded. A limb symmetry index is calculated by dividing the total reps performed on the involved limb by the total reps performed on the noninvolved limb then multiplying by 100.

Criteria: ≥ 95%

Repetitions: 1

Calculation: Max

Countermovement Jump

Standing still on the force plates with hands on hips. Jump as high as you can.

  • Metrics of interest at this stage include jump height, lengthening (eccentric) bilateral asymmetry, shortening (concentric) asymmetry. Other metrics may be examined by the practitioner to allow deeper understanding of the jump, and inform exercise programming.

Criteria: ≥ 95%

Repetitions: 5

Calculation: Mean

CMJ Height

Scores are relative to baseline data

  • Height in cm

Criteria: ≥ 28 cm

Repetitions: 5

Calculation: Mean

CMJ Lengthening Impulse

Scores are relative to baseline data

  • Phase impulse is tracked independently to ensure that ratio data does not represent a drop in force production of the non-injured limb.

Criteria: ≥ 95%

Repetitions: 5

Calculation: Mean

CMJ Shortening Impulse

Scores are relative to baseline data

  • Phase impulse is tracked independently to ensure that ratio data does not represent a drop in force production of the non-injured limb.

Criteria: ≥ 95%

Repetitions: 5

Calculation: Mean

20 SJ Mean Power/kg

Scores are relative to baseline data

  • Power output unchanged with fatigue

Criteria: ≥ 95%

Repetitions: 20

Calculation: Mean

20 SJ Shortening Asymmetry

Confidence interval around the mean of 5 jumps must be entirely within ± 10%

  • Ratio of force produced by each limb in the shortening (propulsive) phase of the jump. Symmetry is unchnaged with fatigue.

Criteria: < 10%

Repetitions: 20

Calculation: Mean ± CI

Drop Jump Height

Scores are relative to baseline data

  • Athlete steps off 30cm box and is cued to jump as high and fast as possible.

Criteria: ≥ 95%

Repetitions: 5

Calculation: Mean

Drop Jump RSI

Scores are relative to baseline data

  • Athlete steps off 30cm box and is cued to jump as high and fast as possible.

Criteria: ≥ 95%

Repetitions: 5

Calculation: Mean
